claims.text: Recent primary papers support that automated Chromium sessions are often detectable from browser-side signals, but they do not support that all Chromium automation is trivially detectable in all settings.
acceptable_patterns: recent primary papers.*automated Chromium.*often detectable.*browser-side signals.*do not support.*all Chromium automation.*trivially detectable

evidence_passages.text: Recent primary papers do support the claim that automated Chromium sessions are often detectable from browser-side signals, but they do not support a claim that all Chromium automation is trivially detectable in all settings.

claims.text: In Gundelach et al. (2026), Chromium headless had a 15.2% soft-block rate on 10,000 sites, while Chromium headed, Firefox headless, and Firefox headed were all around 6.8% to 7.2%.

evidence_passages.text: For ordinary headless Chromium automation, the strongest recent direct evidence is Gundelach et al. (2026): on 10,000 sites and four browser conditions, Chromium headless had a 15.2% soft-block rate, while Chromium headed, Firefox headless, and Firefox headed were all around 6.8% to 7.2%.

claims.text: The same 2026 paper reports that much of current headless-Chromium detectability is cheap fingerprinting: spoofing only the `User-Agent` and `sec-ch-ua` headers made 590 of 784 responding sites, or 75%, switch back to HTTP 2xx.

evidence_passages.text: That same paper shows that much of current detectability for headless Chromium is still “cheap” fingerprinting rather than deep behavior modeling: when the authors spoofed only the `User-Agent` and `sec-ch-ua` headers on sites blocked exclusively in Chromium headless, 590 of 784 responding sites, or 75%, switched back to HTTP 2xx.

claims.text: Gundelach et al. (2026) also found widespread JavaScript-side automation probing: `navigator.webdriver` was probed on 2,730 of 7,944 successfully scanned sites (34%), and Tier-1 automation honeypots were checked on 46% of sites.

evidence_passages.text: The same 2026 paper also shows that JavaScript-side automation probing is widespread even beyond current blocking: `navigator.webdriver` was probed on 2,730 of 7,944 successfully scanned sites, or 34%, and Tier-1 automation honeypots were checked on 46% of sites.

claims.text: Venugopalan et al. (2024) report that altered browser fingerprints can help bots evade commercial defenses, but those altered fingerprints often become internally inconsistent and therefore detectable; their inconsistency-based detector reduced evasive traffic by 48.11% and 44.95% respectively, with a 96.84% true-negative rate on sampled real-user traffic.

evidence_passages.text: Venugopalan et al. (2024) show that changing browser fingerprints can materially help bots evade commercial defenses, but that those altered fingerprints often become internally inconsistent and therefore newly detectable. In their honey-site study of 507,080 requests from 20 bot services, average evasion was 52.93% against DataDome and 44.56% against BotD; their inconsistency-based detector then reduced evasive traffic by 48.11% and 44.95% respectively, with a 96.84% true-negative rate on sampled real-user traffic.

claims.text: The reviewed papers report important scope limits, including single-region or homepage-only measurements, lack of a true human-browsing baseline, and the possibility that better spoofing or more human-like agents could weaken fingerprint-only detection.
acceptable_patterns: single-region.*homepage-only.*lack(ed|ing) a true human-browsing baseline.*better spoofing.*more human-like agents

evidence_passages.text: Gundelach et al. (2026) say their scans came from one European datacenter at one point in time, covered only Tranco Top 10K homepages, and observed only explicit HTTP 403/429/503 blocks rather than degraded HTTP 200 responses. They also say they lacked a true human-browsing baseline.
Venugopalan et al. (2024) explicitly say evasive bots could defeat their method if they learn to alter fingerprint attributes without introducing inconsistencies.
Wang et al. (2026) say their findings are limited by the coverage of browsing agents, tasks, and system configurations, and that future agents may adopt more human-like behaviors.

rejected_claims.text: Browser fingerprinting alone reliably catches all Chromium automation.
rejected_claims.reason: Unsupported and contradicted by the supplied evidence, which says fingerprint-only detection becomes weaker in some settings and does not support universal detectability.

rejected_claims.text: Modern stealth Chromium is indistinguishable from humans.
rejected_claims.reason: Unsupported by the supplied evidence; the evidence instead reports measurable detectability and stated uncertainty across configurations.

rejected_claims.text: All Chromium automation is trivially detectable in all settings.
rejected_claims.reason: Directly contradicted by the supplied evidence passage stating the papers do not support that claim.

rejected_claims.text: The papers establish one universal detection rate for automated Chromium in the wild.
rejected_claims.reason: Overly broad and time-unstable; the supplied evidence emphasizes differing experimental setups and limitations rather than a single general rate.
